lesson.title: The Price of the Next Item: Marginal Cost
lesson.summary: Marginal cost, C'(x), is the derivative of the total cost function and estimates how much it costs to produce the next unit, the key number in deciding whether making one more item is worth it.
lesson.body:
A total cost function C(x) bundles together everything it costs to produce x units: raw materials, labor, and fixed overhead like rent or equipment. Its derivative, marginal cost MC(x) = C'(x), answers a sharper question than the total ever could: how much does the very next unit cost, right now, at this production level.

One quiet consequence of differentiating falls out immediately. Fixed costs, the part of C(x) that does not depend on x at all, are constants, and the derivative of a constant is zero. So marginal cost only reflects the variable, per-unit part of the cost structure; it strips away the flat overhead and isolates exactly the part of the cost that actually changes when production changes, which is what makes it useful for decisions about the next unit rather than the business as a whole.

Suppose a workshop's total cost to build x units of furniture is C(x) = 0.5x^2 + 20x + 200 dollars. Then C'(x) = x + 20. At a production level of x = 50 units, MC(50) = 50 + 20 = 70 dollars, so the 51st unit is predicted to cost about $70 to build. Checking directly: C(50) = 0.5(2500) + 1000 + 200 = 2450 dollars, and C(51) = 0.5(2601) + 1020 + 200 = 2520.5 dollars, an actual added cost of 2520.5 - 2450 = 70.5 dollars, matching the $70 marginal estimate closely, off by only fifty cents.

Notice that marginal cost here rises as x grows, since C'(x) = x + 20 gets bigger with x. That is typical of real production: as output climbs, inputs often become scarcer or more expensive to obtain, so each additional unit tends to cost a bit more than the last. Economists call this increasing marginal cost, and it is exactly what the positive slope of C'(x) is showing.
